01

Screen flow

The artwork is drawn taller than the build plan assumes. Your menu render measures 265 × 687 — an aspect of 0.386, taller than 9:16 (0.563) and taller than any shipping phone. The world is now 720 × 1520 (19:9), which is a real device shape and close enough that the menu needs only a 67 px gutter each side; I filled those with a blurred copy of the same art rather than cropping any of your composition. Screen 2 below is your file, untouched. If the design is meant to be edge-to-edge, it needs redrawing at 19:9 — or the sky band above the logo needs ~170 px of slack that can be cropped.

Splash → Menu → Gameplay ⇄ Pause → Game Over → Skins. One rule shapes all of them: during play the whole screen is the drop target, so nothing touchable sits on the play surface except the pause button, and that lives inside the dead zone.

Resources / items

Resolved by the page-1 asset sheet. The sheet ships a blank wooden sign board and a standalone striped awning as separate pieces, sitting apart from the assembled Coffee storefront. That settles the slicing question: the sign is its own sprite composited over the facade, not painted into it. So a sliced shop scales only the facade while the sign board and awning hold their size, and the shop name stays readable all the way down to MIN_WIDTH. No 9-slice, no rubble fallback, no width threshold.

!

What page 2 changes about the game

Four of the eight families on your sheet describe mechanics the build plan does not have. Flagging them rather than absorbing them quietly, because together they are the difference between an 11-day build and something closer to five weeks.

Art on the sheetMechanic it impliesIn the plan?Cost

The one that's pure upside

The three sky plates cost nothing mechanically and make progress legible at a glance — you know how well you're doing by what time it is. No balance, no data, no new screens. Already wired into the live loop.

Shipped in this build. Watch the Sky readout climb DAY → SUNSET → NIGHT.

The four that change the product

Hearts, levels, upgrades and crafting turn a 20-second endless stacker into a level-based builder with an economy. That is a real game, and BUILD. UPGRADE. CONQUER supports it — but it is not the game the milestones cost, and it needs balance work that only shows up after launch.

+14 days on top of the 11, and the risk sits in tuning, not code.

What I'd do

Ship the endless stacker with the full page-1 and page-2 art, the sky progression and skins. Hold hearts, levels, upgrades and crafting for a 1.1 you only build if retention justifies it. Hyper-casual data generally favours the endless version, and a thin meta layer on a game nobody reopens is wasted work.

Want the meta layer in v1 instead? Say so and I'll re-cost M0–M5 properly.

Do not let this get decided by an asset sheet. Every icon here is cheap to draw and expensive to make work — a heart costs an hour of art and a week of refill-timer balancing. Pick the game first, then commission only the art that game needs.

Page 1 — sprite inventory

Every piece the splash decomposes into, at export size for a 1080-wide device (world 720 → 1.5×). Reusable marks the pieces that pay for themselves across all twelve shops — those three rows are why a new skin costs a facade, not a storefront.

SpriteExport pxCopiesUsed byNote

Atlas budget. That is roughly 3.2 M pixels of art. It packs into a single 2048 × 2048 page at about 76% fill — workable but tight, so if the packer struggles, drop the facade export to 512 × 180 first; it is the row that dominates. Quantised, the whole sheet should land near 1.5–2.5 MB, comfortably inside the 12 MB install target.

Still open on page 1. The splash shows the logo hanging from the crane, which means the logo lockup and the crane rig have to share a vertical axis on every aspect ratio from 16:9 to 21:9. Pin the rig to screen centre and let the tower art below it letterbox — do not scale the rig with the safe area, or the cable detaches from the clamp on tall phones.

Core palette

04

Slice math, checked in this page

Not transcribed — this table runs resolve() in your browser, on the same function the phone above is using, and asserts three invariants per row: containment, width conservation (kept + offcut = previous, exactly), and non-overlap of the offcut. Drop it straight into tests/towerRules.spec.ts. The re-skin to shops changed nothing here — that is the point of keeping core/ Phaser-free.

Caseprev x, wtap xoutcomenew xnew woffcut xoffcut winvariants

The fairness floor is a feel decision in disguise. A miss is ovW <= MIN_WIDTH, not ovW <= 0. Ending a run on a 20 px sliver reads as fair; ending it on a 0.4 px hairline reads as a bug — and with shop art, a sliver narrower than the door is unreadable anyway.

05

Tunables

One GameConfig.ts, nothing magic-numbered into a scene. Live means the phone above is running it. Two constants moved when the theme changed from bare blocks to storefronts — both marked changed.

ConstantValueUnitControlsStatus

Your two references disagree about shop shape, and it changes the game. The standalone sprites are portrait — measured across all thirteen they run 0.72 to 0.89 wide-to-tall, averaging 0.79. But the gameplay screen on page 2 draws the stacked shops landscape, roughly 2:1, which is how it fits five or six on screen. Both cannot be true. This build honours the sprites, because you asked for the exact assets: BLOCK_HEIGHT 280, START_WIDTH 230, giving 4.6 shops on screen and a block 32% of the screen wide. If you want the page-2 density instead, the art has to be redrawn landscape — squashing these vertically will not survive the slicing.

Slicing is a horizontal 3-slice, not a squash. The outer 30% of each sprite is pinned at natural scale so the planters and pilasters never distort; only the middle band stretches. A shop sliced to a sliver keeps its doorway and its plants, which is exactly why the art holds up as the tower narrows.

Why BLOCK_HEIGHT went 60 → 140. A storefront needs a sign, an awning and a facade to read as a shop; at 60 px world it reads as a stripe. At 140 you get about nine shops on screen and roughly five above the base before the camera starts following — which is exactly the density in the reference. The cost is that the tower reads slower, so SPEED_STEP may want to come up to 10.

→

What I need from you before M1

Five calls, ordered by how expensive they get to reverse.

Does the drop feel right?

Play thirty seconds on your phone. PERFECT_EPS 6 and BASE_SPEED 260 are the two numbers everything hangs off, and the only ones I can't pick for you.

Too forgiving → EPS 4. Too punishing → 8, and raise GROW.

Who draws the twelve shops?

The CSS versions above are a stand-in that proves the layout, not shippable art. Twelve painted storefronts plus a sky/city parallax plate is roughly a week of an illustrator's time, and it is the single biggest thing standing between this and the reference.

Cheapest real path: buy a casual-shop asset pack, recolour to this palette.

Coins — or just score?

The skins screen shows a 120 coin balance, which implies an earn rate, a sink, and a balance to tune. Score-threshold unlocks plus rewarded video need none of that.

Recommend: ship v1 on thresholds + rewarded. Add coins in 1.1 if skins pull.

Confirm the ad floor

No banner during play — the whole screen is the drop target, so a banner near it means accidental clicks, and sustained accidental clicks suspend AdMob accounts. Interstitial every 3rd game over, 60 s minimum gap, one rewarded Continue per run.

This is a policy call as much as a design one.

Slice behaviour on the art

Answer the 9-slice question from section 2 and I can lock the atlas. Everything else in the build plan is unaffected by it; this one is not.

Default if you don't pick: 9-slice with a fixed 64 px sign, generic block under 90 px.
